reference.title: Barbell Front Rack Lunge
reference.listing: Page not read (gymvisual.com blocked by the proxy); movement taken from the exercise name and standard coaching
reference.note: Reference used only to identify the movement. No GymVisual media is stored here; this rig, model and animation are original.

breathing.pattern: Big breath and brace before you step; hold it down and through the hardest part of the push back, then breathe out at the top.
breathing.cadence: About 1.6 s step and lower, short pause, about 1.7 s push back

prescription.tempo: Controlled step, 1-2 s down, push back in about 1 s
prescription.progression: Heavier bar in small steps, then walking or deficit lunges. Barbell load is user-chosen: pick a weight that leaves about 2-3 reps in reserve (RPE 7-8) at the end of each set.

cues.text: Unrack the bar into the front rack: bar across the front of the shoulders, in the fingers just outside the shoulders, elbows forward and up, chest tall.
Brace and take a long step forward with the right foot, heel first; keep the elbows up.
Drop straight down until the front knee is about 90 degrees and the back knee is just above the floor; trunk stays upright.
Drive through the front heel and step back to standing without letting the elbows drop.
Stand tall and reset the rack; alternate legs or finish the set on one side.

mistakes.fix: Lead with the elbows up; if the bar rolls forward, the load or the grip is too much.
Keep the chest tall; the bar in front should sit over mid-foot of the front leg.

mistakes.mistake: Step too short, front knee shooting far past the toes with the heel lifting
mistakes.fix: Take a longer step and keep the whole front foot down.

mistakes.mistake: Back knee slamming into the floor
mistakes.fix: Lower under control and stop just above the floor.

kinematics.peak: 80 cm forward (72.2 cm between ankle centres once the back heel is up)
kinematics.norm: Front knee about over the front foot at the bottom (common guideline); about one leg length was suggested as optimal in the split squat (Song 2023)
About 90 degrees at the bottom (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: ≈102°, 14 cm above the floor (knee joint centre)
kinematics.norm: Lowers to just above the floor, about 90 degrees (clinical opinion)
Upright; a front-loaded bar keeps the trunk more vertical than a back-loaded one (Gullett 2009, squat), and more lean shifts work to the hip extensors (Farrokhi 2008)

kinematics.setup: Bar across the front delts in the fingers, 67 cm between the hands (handle points); upper arms ≈35° below horizontal, elbows 18.6 cm in front of the shoulder joints; wrists extended 90°
kinematics.peak: Unchanged: the bar rides with the trunk (grip width 67.44-67.44 cm), 81.16 cm min plate height
kinematics.norm: Bar across the front delts in the fingers, hands just outside the shoulders, elbows forward and up; the bar should not rest on the throat or collarbones (clinical opinion)

kinematics.peak: Step 0.8 s, 1.0 s down, 0.3 s pause, 0.75 s up, step back 0.85 s
kinematics.norm: Controlled, about 1-2 s down and 1 s up (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #7584, Barbell Front Rack Lunge, video (movement reference)
Hip, knee and ankle joint moments in the single-legged squat, forward lunge and reverse lunge (J Athl Train; PMC4641539)
Farrokhi et al. 2008, trunk position influences lead-leg kinematics, kinetics and muscle activity in the forward lunge (J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 38:403-409)
Song et al. 2023, effects of step lengths on lower-extremity biomechanics during the split squat (Front Bioeng Biotechnol 11:1277493)
Gullett, Tillman, Gutierrez & Chow 2009, a biomechanical comparison of back and front squats in healthy trained individuals (J Strength Cond Res 23(1):284-292; PubMed 19002072)

cautions: Unrack from a squat rack at about shoulder height; set the bar back in the rack when you finish. Step back far enough to clear the uprights.
If you lose balance, step the front foot back and drop the bar forward away from the body rather than fighting it.
The bar rests on the muscle of the front shoulders, not on the throat or collarbones; ease off if the front rack hurts the wrists or chokes you.
Stop if sharp pain, numbness, tingling or giving-way occurs.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Stiff wrists: a fingertip rack or a slightly wider grip; straps around the bar are another option.
Knee pain: a shorter range, or a reverse lunge (stepping back).
Balance: stand with the feet a little wider (on train tracks, not a tightrope).
regressions: Goblet reverse lunge with a dumbbell.
Dumbbell lunge with the weights at the sides.
progressions: Front rack lunge from a small deficit.

muscleNotes.quads_r: Front-leg knee extensors brake the step and drive the push back.
muscleNotes.quads_l: Front-leg knee extensors brake the step and drive the push back.
muscleNotes.glute_max_r: Front-leg hip extensor; hip moments were greater in the forward lunge than in the reverse lunge (PMC4641539), and more so with the trunk inclined forward (Farrokhi 2008).
muscleNotes.glute_max_l: Front-leg hip extensor; hip moments were greater in the forward lunge than in the reverse lunge (PMC4641539), and more so with the trunk inclined forward (Farrokhi 2008).
muscleNotes.adductors_r: Adductor magnus assists hip extension and steadies the thigh.
muscleNotes.adductors_l: Adductor magnus assists hip extension and steadies the thigh.
muscleNotes.hamstrings_r: Assist hip extension and co-contract around the front knee.
muscleNotes.hamstrings_l: Assist hip extension and co-contract around the front knee.
muscleNotes.calves_r: Steady the front shin; the back calf holds the heel up.
muscleNotes.calves_l: Steady the front shin; the back calf holds the heel up.
muscleNotes.glute_med_r: Keeps the pelvis level and the front knee over the toes on the narrow base.
muscleNotes.glute_med_l: Keeps the pelvis level and the front knee over the toes on the narrow base.
muscleNotes.core: Braces the trunk under a front-loaded bar; the load in front of the trunk asks the abdominals and back to keep the chest up (clinical opinion; front loading kept the trunk more upright than back loading in the squat, Gullett 2009).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_r: Hold the trunk upright against the bar in front; a front-loaded squat needed less trunk lean and no more back extensor demand than the back squat (Gullett 2009).
muscleNotes.spinal_extensors_l: Hold the trunk upright against the bar in front; a front-loaded squat needed less trunk lean and no more back extensor demand than the back squat (Gullett 2009).
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_r: Keep the upper back from rounding forward under the bar (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_l: Keep the upper back from rounding forward under the bar (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_r: The front delts form the shelf the bar rests on; keeping the elbows up holds it there (clinical opinion).
muscleNotes.ant_deltoid_l: The front delts form the shelf the bar rests on; keeping the elbows up holds it there (clinical opinion).
